item.title: Guam Board of Education chair wants oversight hearing on Public Health's requirements for schools
item.description: Guam Board of Education Chairperson Judith Guthertz said Monday she would like the chair of the Legislature’s Committee on Education to call an immediate oversight hearing for the Department of Public Health’s Environmental Health Division. Guthertz said she was upset because people on a radio talk show were making fun of the Education Department for installing air conditioning in school restrooms
item.content:encoded:
Guam Board of Education Chairperson Judith Guthertz said Monday she would like the chair of the Legislature’s Committee on Education to call an immediate oversight hearing for the Department of Public Health’s Environmental Health Division.

Guthertz said she was upset because people on a radio talk show were making fun of the Education Department for installing air conditioning in school restrooms, but the department is merely complying with Public Health regulations.

She said the oversight hearing should be called, “with the goal of determining whether or not these regulations make sense. That is the source of many of the difficulties that we have experienced over the last few months.”

The Tiyan High School campus, which also housed students from Simon Sanchez High School, was closed by Public Health shortly after the school year began in August, leading to double sessions and emergency repairs.

She wanted the public to know the idea for cooler bathrooms did not come from the Education Department.

“People in the community don't understand this, that we have to honor those regulations, no matter whether or not they make sense,” she said, questioning whether air conditioning in restrooms would affect student learning. “I take great exception to the lack of clarification on the part of the media that do not understand where these regulations come from.”

She said air conditioning is also being installed at University of Guam restrooms.

“Can you imagine what the costs are going to be for DOE? We have to do this in every school, in every bathroom, and at the university and at GCC. Why could we not put ceiling fans? Would that not help?” she asked. “Split units, the cost of retrofitting the electrical requirements, the installation costs, the material costs, the equipment costs. I'd rather use that money in the classrooms.”

Because the matter could not be addressed during Monday’s emergency meeting for the department’s spending plan, Guthertz asked that it be placed on the board agenda for the upcoming Nov. 17 meeting.

The board will consider whether to ask the superintendent to request an oversight hearing on the Public Health requirements.

item.title: DPW announces Simon Sanchez High School project to move forward through two separate procurement processes
item.description: The Department of Public Works announced that the Simon Sanchez High School project is moving forward through two separate procurement processes, but neither demolition nor construction has officially begun. item.content:encoded:
The Department of Public Works announced that the Simon Sanchez High School project is moving forward through two separate procurement processes, but neither demolition nor construction has officially begun.

Under the first procurement process, Public Works has completed its part of the bidding process for demolishing the existing Simon Sanchez High School Campus, and the Office of the Attorney General has reviewed and cleared the demolition bid documents. However, Public Works is still waiting for GDOE to authorize the architect, TRMA, to finish the remaining work and release the documents needed. Once GDOE accepts, Public Works says it is ready to advertise the demolition bidding and move forward.

For the second procurement and the construction of the new school, Public Works has completed preparing the request for proposals for the school’s construction through a public-private partnership. The proposal package still needs final review by the Attorney General's Office before it is issued. Public Works plans to turn over the procurement package to the incoming administration for consideration and implementation.

item.title: Selection committee to interview six MVA director candidates
item.description: The Marianas Visitors Authority board of directors has formed a selection committee to evaluate six applicants for the agency's vacant managing director position. The action came during a special board meeting Monday where directors addressed the recently closed job vacancy announcement for MVA's top executive post.
item.content:encoded:
The Marianas Visitors Authority board of directors has formed a selection committee to evaluate six applicants for the agency's vacant managing director position.

The action came during a special board meeting Monday where directors addressed the recently closed job vacancy announcement for MVA's top executive post.

Acting Managing Director Judy Torres told board members that the application period ended last week.

The board approved the creation of a selection committee tasked with reviewing applications, conducting interviews and recommending a candidate to the full board.

The committee consists of board members Sakuro Gerrard, Chris Nelson and Joe Guerrero, along with Torres and MVA Human Resources Manager Tina Matsunaga.

Acting Board Chair Vicky Benavente said the committee will begin its work as soon as possible.

"The selection committee will meet as soon as possible and conduct interviews and evaluations and will make a recommendation to the whole board," Benavente said.

Speaking with reporters following the meeting, Torres declined to identify the applicants.

Asked whether MVA has established a target date for hiring its next managing director, Torres said the timeline will depend on how quickly the committee can complete its review process.

"It all depends on how soon the committee can review the applications and set up a date to proceed," she said.

No timeline for a final hiring decision was announced.

item.title: Thick smog shrouds New Delhi after Diwali firecrackers add to seasonal pollution

item.content:encoded:
NEW DELHI — A thick blanket of smog shrouded India's capital Monday after firecrackers lit up the skies over New Delhi during Diwali celebrations, compounding dangerously high pollution levels and intensifying the seasonal air pollution crisis that grips the city every year.

Despite restrictions on fireworks, residents in New Delhi celebrated the Hindu festival of lights with firecrackers on Sunday evening, releasing smoke and fine particulate matter into the atmosphere. The air quality index exceeded 350 in several parts of the capital on Monday morning, reaching the severe category and posing significant health risks.

Monitoring stations across the city recorded similarly alarming levels, while visibility deteriorated as a gray haze blanketed streets and high-rise buildings.

India's Supreme Court in October had sought to limit Diwali pollution by restricting conventional firecrackers and allowing only approved "green firecrackers" under specified conditions for three-hour windows on Saturday and Sunday. The crackers produce fewer emissions but are not pollution-free. They still release particulate matter and other pollutants, adding to the city's already hazardous air.

Isyad, a New Delhi resident who uses one name, said the worsening smog was taking a toll on his health.

"Because of the pollution there is irritation in the throat and itching in the eyes," he said.

New Delhi and its metropolitan region, home to more than 30 million people, regularly rank among the world's most polluted areas during winter. Pollution worsens as Diwali fireworks coincide with cooler weather and smoke from crop-residue fires in neighboring states of Punjab and Haryana.

After harvesting rice, farmers often burn leftover stalks to clear their fields for the next planting season. The smoke drifts toward New Delhi, adding to pollution from vehicles, industries, construction dust and other local sources.

The problem becomes particularly acute in late October and November, when cooler temperatures, low wind speeds and stagnant atmospheric conditions prevent pollutants from dispersing. The result is a thick haze that can linger over the capital and surrounding areas for days.

Authorities in New Delhi have implemented a set of measures to curb pollution, which include limits on construction activity and restrictions on diesel generators, while courts have sough restrictions on firecrackers. But the measures have not prevented the return of severe pollution each year.

Environmentalists say long-term solutions, such as cleaner energy and stricter controls on vehicle emissions, are needed to prevent the annual crisis.

Shweta Narayan, a public health expert at the Global Climate and Health Alliance, described the government's response so far as "knee-jerk" and "temporary."

"A lot of interventions happen only because the government is pressured or pushed in a corner to do something," she said.

item.title: British comedian Russell Brand sentenced to over 10 years for rape and sexual assault
item.description: Russell Brand, the raunchy, irreverent British comedian who became a celebrity darling in the early 2000s, has been sentenced to over 10 years in prison after being found guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. "The total sentence is one of ten years, six months," said Judge Justice Bennathan on handing down the sentence at Southwark Crown Court in London on Monday.
item.content:encoded:
Russell Brand, the raunchy, irreverent British comedian who became a celebrity darling in the early 2000s, has been sentenced to over 10 years in prison after being found guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

"The total sentence is one of ten years, six months," said Judge Justice Bennathan on handing down the sentence at Southwark Crown Court in London on Monday.

Brand, 51, was a career chameleon who went from stand-up comic and MTV host to a political analyst esteemed by Britain's left, only to become a conspiracy theorist and Christian convert beloved by the U.S. right.

But critics of Brand said there was always a clear thread of misogyny running through his comedy routines, and that his mistreatment of women had been an open secret for decades.

Over the past four weeks, six women testified against the comedian in court in London, in a trial that garnered massive media attention.

A jury found Brand guilty last week on four of the seven counts against him. He was found guilty of raping a woman he'd met at one of his shows in 2009 and of sexually assaulting three women — at a bar, a radio station and a TV studio — between 2004 and 2009.

Brand denies all charges and said he never had non-consensual sex.

Before the judge handed down the sentence, four of the women who brought the case against Brand gave victim impact statements to the court. Three of the statements were read out by the prosecution, while one woman appeared in court behind a curtain to read her own.

None of the women have been publicly named and the trial was not televised.

The prosecution read out an impact statement from the one complainant, who Brand was found guilty of anally raping at his home in 2009. In her statement she said: "It's something I carry with me every day and it often feels never-ending."

"I doubt my ability to make good decisions and no longer trust my instinct in the way I did," her statement said, adding that because of Brand's fame she didn't think she'd be believed if she reported him.

Another complainant, who Brand was found guilty of sexually assaulting at a bar in 2004 when he grabbed her breasts, said the confusion of what she "should" or "could" do had stayed with her for over 20 years.

The complainant, who spoke in person from behind a curtain in the courtroom, said she felt "physically sick" seeing Brand in the press afterwards as his fame rose.

Another of Brand's victims, who he was found guilty of sexually assaulting in 2005, said the assault had "a lasting impact on her life" and that over the years "hearing his voice on television or seeing his image has made me jump."

A fourth woman, who Brand was found guilty of sexually assaulting when they worked together at a TV studio, said she was badly affected and afterwards felt her working environment was unsafe.

British media who were in the court for the sentencing said Brand, who had spent the weekend in prison, was in the suit he was convicted in on Thursday and sat holding a set of white rosary beads as the victim statements were read. Brand's wife Laura, who had supported him throughout the case, was in court, as was his father.

After the victim statements, the defense and prosecution teams had the opportunity to make their last statements.

The prosecution called for a long sentence, saying there were aggravating circumstances in the anal rape case, such as Brand removing a condom. The defence meanwhile said Brand was "a fundamentally different person" from who he was at the time of the crimes.

After considering the victim impact statements and those by the defence and prosecution, the judge handed down the sentence live on camera.

In his remarks, he said Brand had become "a sexual predator" and paused "to pay tribute to the determination and bravery" of the women who'd come forward.

He then ordered Brand to be taken down to the cells.

item.title: Why a South Korean city is turning to a U.S. college to outsmart AI?
item.description: CHUNCHEON, South Korea — "Is the Frankenstein monster human?" a teacher asks students at the Toegye public elementary school in Chuncheon city, some 50 miles east of Seoul, as they discuss Mary Shelley's novel Frankenstein . "I think we can call it a human being with no soul," ventures student Ma Yeonwoo.
item.content:encoded:
CHUNCHEON, South Korea — "Is the Frankenstein monster human?" a teacher asks students at the Toegye public elementary school in Chuncheon city, some 50 miles east of Seoul, as they discuss Mary Shelley's novel Frankenstein .

"I think we can call it a human being with no soul," ventures student Ma Yeonwoo.

The Toegye school has adopted the " Great Books" educational model used by St. John's College, whose main campus is in Annapolis, Md.

The class's discussion then shifts to whether artificial intelligence is human.

"No," Ma Yeonwoo responds, because humans created AI, and although it is intelligent, it "has no creativity."

In the "Great Books" model, teachers do not lecture, they only guide discussions. There are no majors or elective courses. Students do not seek answers from outside sources such as the internet and rely only on their readings, their own reasoning and class discussions with their peers.

That suits Ma Yeonwoo, who says he enjoys debating with his classmates.

"If only the teacher talks we can have one idea, but if we all debate together, like, we can get many ideas together," he says.

This nascent educational movement addresses several concerning trends. One is that international tests such as PISA have shown a post-COVID drop in South Korean reading skills, after decades in which South Korean and other East Asian students outperformed their American counterparts.

Another is South Korea's rapid adoption of AI in education. 51% of South Korean students say they use AI chatbots to study at least once a week, according to Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) figures. Students also face intense competition to pass college entrance exams, which piles pressure on them down to the pre-K school level and prompts many South Korean families to send their children to cram schools to gain a competitive edge, or to foreign schools to escape the system.

"We all feel that this system leaves students with no time to read and think," because they're too busy memorizing facts to pass tests," says Lee Yonghwa, a professor of English language and literature at Incheon National University, where he co-founded South Korea's first "Great Books" program in 2019.

But now, Lee laments, "Korean students are even losing their old capacity to memorize facts because they collect facts and ideas mainly from A.I."

And if they can't reason and think independently, he adds, they can't judge the quality of the results that AI generates for them.

The limitations of their educational system motivates many South Koreans to look for alternatives, from education overseas, to educational experiments at home.

"As someone who went through this system, I felt those limitations keenly," Chuncheon Mayor Yook Dong-han said in an interview at city hall. "When I became mayor, I wanted to introduce a different kind of education and a distinct educational philosophy to the city of Chuncheon."

Chuncheon draws visitors from neighboring Seoul to enjoy its mountains, lakes and rivers, and dakgalbi, a local dish of grilled or stir-fried marinated chicken.

Chuncheon's government established an academic partnership with St. John's College last year to promote the "Great Books" educational model.

There are now 120 college students and some 770 younger students taking the "Great Books" program in South Korea, and 40 teachers in training, according to Lee Yonghwa.

Although the program is still in its infancy, Yook says it represents a "small but revolutionary achievement — a breakthrough that challenges established practices," and generated interest among participating students that has exceeded his expectations.

South Korean students following the "Great Books" model read Aristotle, Shakespeare, Euclid, and Korean authors including Nobel laureate Han Kang .

In one Chuncheon high school, students read Martin Luther King Jr.'s 1963 Letter from Birmingham Jail .

They discuss King's ideas about what kind of laws are just and unjust, and which laws citizens should obey or disobey.

Lee Yonghwa says he's impressed that students connected King's letter to their own country, such as in 2024, when citizens and lawmakers defeated former President Yoon Suk Yeol's attempt to put South Korea under martial law.

That fits the purpose of the "Great Books" model, in which "each seminar table really becomes a miniature republic, where ideas clash but people cooperate," St. John's College President J. Walter Sterling wrote last year in an opinion essay .

Through civic participation and liberal education, he adds, "we quietly stitch the fabric of our democracy…before it unravels beyond repair."

NPR's Se Eun Gong contributed to this report in Chuncheon and Seoul.

item.title: Democrats won big on issues like immigration. But ICE still has the money
item.description: In the days leading up to the midterm elections, hundreds of people left their "I voted" stickers on a memorial for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo , a Houston man killed by federal immigration agents earlier this year. "The fact that people were thinking of my dad and thinking of other immigrants — that just means the world to me," said Ronaldo Salgado, Salgado Araujo's son, told NPR.
item.content:encoded:
In the days leading up to the midterm elections, hundreds of people left their "I voted" stickers on a memorial for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo , a Houston man killed by federal immigration agents earlier this year.

"The fact that people were thinking of my dad and thinking of other immigrants — that just means the world to me," said Ronaldo Salgado, Salgado Araujo's son, told NPR.

Those votes resulted in a seismic political shift in Texas: for the first time, a Latina, Democrat Gina Hinojosa , will be governor. Texans also elected the state's first Democratic U.S. senator in nearly 40 years, and the Texas House of Representatives flipped .

"Unfortunately, Texas has become like the epicenter of ICE enforcement and like gross violence against immigrants," Ronaldo Salgado said. "Well, the voters have spoken — incoming lawmakers now have a duty to listen to us."

Immigration policy was one of the top issues on voters' minds this election, according to exit polling . Artemio Muñiz of the Texas Federation of Hispanic Republicans, told NPR "with these anti-immigrant-type policies, I think the Hispanic community got fed up."

That seems more true than ever in the counties along the U.S.-Mexico border, which flipped Democratic after supporting Trump in 2024.

"I think the message is clear from the Texas Hispanic community that the only acceptable or effective Hispanic outreach from the Republican Party in Texas is one that includes a reasonable solution for immigration," Muñiz said, suggesting the solution should include secured borders and a legal pathway for undocumented immigrants who have been in the U.S. for decades.

In Texas, Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa is facing calls to end the state's partnership with ICE.

"That's something that can happen on day one," said César Espinosa, the executive director of the Houston-based advocacy organization FIEL. He said his group would also like to see Hinojosa and the Texas legislature to push for driver licenses for undocumented immigrants. Already, Houston's mayor is reducing his police department's cooperation with ICE.

Nationwide, immigration advocates say they want to see ICE defunded, or severely restricted.

"We demand that the incoming Congress hold ICE accountable", says Murad Awawdeh of the New York Immigrant Coalition.

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is set to become the next chair of the House oversight committee, had two words of advice for Republicans on Election Day: "Lawyer up."

Garcia has promised to look into several issues, including ICE accountability.

ICE is the highest funded federal law enforcement agency in the U.S. Congress essentially gave immigration enforcement a blank check in 2025 and in 2026 they awarded ICE and Customs and Border Patrol around $240 billion.

It's enough funds to run the mass deportation operation for the remainder of Trump's term.

Congress could claw back that money. And lawmakers are already eyeing more stringent oversight.

"We have to rein ICE in because its illegal, out-of-control activities (have) killed individuals … assaulted individuals … have incarcerated individuals," said Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., who is likely to chair the House Homeland Security Committee. "That system has to have accountability for the men and women who work in it."

He said he'd like to legally require policies, like requiring the use of body-worn cameras for federal immigration agents and banning them from wearing face coverings.

The major hurdle is President Trump: following the midterm election results the President said he would welcome the nickname "Mr. Veto."

Another possible indication of how the administration will be seeing immigration enforcement moving forward came Friday , a few days after the midterm elections. White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller was promoted to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Miller's central project in government has been immigration control and mass deportations. Miller is considered the architect of the first Trump administration's child separation policy, and as NPR reported, was deeply involved in the project of turning large warehouses into immigration detention centers.

Naureen Shah at the ACLU says she thinks one of the most powerful things that could happen to change ICE behavior is Congressional oversight via subpoenas.

"ICE has to be afraid," she said. "They have to be afraid of losing their funding, they have to be afraid of being subpoenaed and asked extremely hard questions before a live audience of the American people."

The day after the Midterm elections, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin posted a three-word tweet : " Deportations will continue ."

Vice President JD Vance took to X to share his thoughts on the Republican Party's big loss. He said he believes it is due to voter's concerns over the economy, inflation and the war with Iran. He left immigration enforcement off that list.

He did, however, say he is open to changing enforcement tactics by focusing more on businesses that hire undocumented workers. But he said immigration amnesty is not the solution.

Shah of the ACLU says she believes ICE enforcement and the current state of the economy are inextricably linked. "What's really clear is that the stories of life becoming harder for everyday Americans are actually also stories about ICE's impact. People are afraid to take their kids to school, afraid to go to work. It impacts our schools, our teachers. It impacts the labor force when people aren't showing up for their jobs. So Democrats have an opportunity through their oversight device to tell a story about how to make everyday life more affordable for all Americans."

The Trump administration has spent billions of dollars to expand ICE detention facilities — many of which have faced criticism and protest over dire conditions. There have been a record number of deaths in detention since the start of Trump's second term.

The day after mid-term election results the two major private detention center companies that contract for ICE, CoreCivic and the GEO Group , had their quarterly investor calls.

The main question asked by investors at the CoreCivic call was: how will the result of the midterms affect ICE operations?

CoreCivic President Lucibeth Mayberry optimistically, pointing out that "[ICE] have again began increasing enforcement activity. They have the secure funding to do so." But then she offered a word of advice to ICE about purchasing new detention centers: "we would urge the ICE administration to move quickly."
